This general was undefeated in battles like Issus during their conquest of the Persian Achaemenid(a-KEE-ma-nid) Empire. For 10 points, name this "great" king of Macedon.

Artifacts used in this practice, including a dragon-headed plaque made of whalebone, were found at the site of Scar in Orkney. The consumption of alcohol by a slave girl, who went from tent to tent to have intercourse with several men, was described in an account of this practice by Ibn Fadlan. In 2017, Annika Larsson controversially claimed that the embroidery on clothing used in this practice contained words in Kufic script reading "Ali" and "Allah." Oval-shaped "stone ships," like one found near the Jelling ("yelling") stones, marked places used for this practice. A helmet adorned with boar motifs that matched descriptions in (*) Beowulf was found at a site where this practice took place named Sutton Hoo. Contrary to popular depictions, these events did not involve setting fire to a vessel at sea. For 10 points, identify this practice in which Vikings and their ships were lowered underground.

Numerous Sufi khanqahs ("kaan-kaas") were constructed as a result of Muhammad bin Tughluq's ("TOOG-looks") foolish efforts to perform this type of action in 1327, which failed due to a lack of water. Due to 1961's incredibly destructive Hurricane Hattie, George Cadle Price lobbied for English support to undertake this type of project in Belize. The Portuguese architecture firm FAT is spearheading one of these projects in Equatorial Guinea that is intended to give more (*) political power to the people of the Rio Muni region. One effort of this type involved a city known as the "window to Europe" being constructed upon the Neva River by a certain Tsar. For 10 points, Peter the Great performed what action that resulted in St. Petersburg eclipsing Moscow as the seat of the Russian government?
2.r: moving to a new capital [accept building a new capital, switching tu 21capitals, or anything illustrating the creation of a new capital; prompt on migration with “Migrating to where?”; prompt on building a road with “Where did that road lead to?”; prompt on building a city with “What type of city?"]
2.c: 2019 Florida Spring Tournament (FST) Pkt G. Packet 7 Q20

2.q: The accusation that Aulus Licinius Archias had not been subjected to this action led to his student Cicero defending him in the oration Pro Archia Poeta. The younger Marcus Livius Drusus was assassinated for supporting a bill that would have performed this action. This action was performed in places such as Etruria by a 90 BC Lex Julia as a reward to allied towns. Gaius Gracchus proposed a bill that would have performed this action, which was rejected by plebeians who feared competition for the grain dole, and was a major cause behind the (*) Social War. This action was carried out through the Constitutio Antoniniana, which mostly applied to those living outside of Italy. For 10 points, name this action most notably carried out by Caracalla in 212 AD, which granted full rights to residents of all provinces within his empire.
2.r: expanding Roman citizenship [accept descriptive answers that mention becoming a citizen of Rome such as granting citizenship or giving citizenship; prompt on just citizenship by asking “what action is occurring?”; prompt on becoming Roman by asking “in what way?”]

2.q: The Primary Chronicle, or the Tale of Bygone Years, is a history of this city that chronicles its mythical founding by the brothers Khi, Schek, and Khoryv.(KOR-iv). During a 1240 invasion of this city by the Mongols, citizens attempted to shelter in this city's Church of the Tithes until it collapsed. A state that ruled from this city was founded by Oleg the Wise, the son of legendary Varangian (*) Rurik. This city's prince Vladimir the Great held a mass baptism in the Dnieper River. (NEE-per river). The Mongols ended a state centered on this city that was ruled by the Rus'. (rhymes with loose). For 10 points, name this capital of Ukraine.

Charles C. Mann visits a region in this country at the beginning of 1491 while being led around by two members of its Siriono people. The Labyrinthian building of Chinkana is among the pre-Colombian sites on this country's Isla del Sol. A site known as "The Door of the Puma" is part of a complex built by a people in this country who also built the "Gate to the Sun." The Wiphala ["wee-pah-lah"] flag, a flag of a people primarily in this country, had its (*) Qullasuyu ["koo-ya-soo-yoo"] version adopted as this country's dual flag. This country, home to a pre-Colombian site constructed by the Tiwanaku, was home to silver mining centered at Cerro Rico, which necessitated the building of a massive National Mint in this country's city of Potosi. For 10 points, name this country, which shares Lake Titicaca with Peru.
2.r: Plurinational State of Bolivia [or Estado Plurinacional de Bolivia]

2.q: Agricola won the Battle of Mons Graupius in the far northernmost portion of this island, which emperor Septimus Severus died while campaigning in. This island was home to the Iceni ("ice-see-nee") tribe, who were crushed at the Battle of Watling Street. The Caledonian confederacy was located on this island, as were a group possibly named for their extensive tattoos, the (*) Picts. Emperor Hadrian constructed a 73-mile long defensive wall spanning this island. Boudica's revolt occurred in this island, whose Celtic population split into groups including the Cornish and Bretons. For 10 points, name this island on which the settlement of Londinium later became the city of London.

A city in this modern-day country was the capital of the Yamhad kingdom and was renamed Beroea after it was conquered by Alexander the Great. This country's capital was the northern end of the Decapolis according to Pliny. A city in this country worshiped the triad of Bel, Yarhibol, and Agribol. The Seleucid and Ptolemaic empires fought over a region called 'Coele-[this country's name].' Odaenathus ruled a city in this country that fought against (*) Aurelian under its queen Zenobia, Palmyra. This country was the site of Ramesses II's alleged victory over the Hittites at Kadesh. This country has the oldest capital city in the world, which gives its name to swords made of wootz steel. For 10 points, name this country whose ancient cities include Aleppo and Damascus.

This man put down a revolt by Ambiorix in Belgae territory. This man used a military donut in the Battle of Alesia to defeat forces led by Vercingetorix. As Pontifex Maximus, this man reformed the calendar to add leap years. This man wrote about Druids in his (*) Commentaries on the Gallic War. This man's refusal to give up command culminated in his crossing of the Rubicon in 49 BCE, leading to the start of a civil war. This man posthumously adopted Gaius Octavius, later known as Octavian. For 10 points, name this Roman general who was stabbed to death on the Ides of March.

In a book on this city, Patricia Crone argued against traditional accounts of it as a trade hub. French GIGN commandos backed up one country's forces during a siege of this city perpetrated by followers of the Salafist Abd al-Aziz ibn Baz. Abraha's attempted entrance to this city failed when his lead elephant refused to move, ending an Aksumite invasion of it. Leaders of this city claimed to be descendants of Banu Hashim and were also known as the (*) hejaz. Forces loyal to this city lost to a religious group in the Battle of Badr after which they signed the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, allowing the Quraysh pilgrimage to this city. Muhammad went to Medina during the Hijra, a flight from, for 10 points, what city, the holiest in Islam?

According to Suetonius, Ptolemy of Mauretania was killed by Caligula for showing off his ownership of this good. Julius Pollux claimed that this good was discovered when Hercules' dog was sniffing around on the beach. It's not glass, but Sidon was a production center for this good. Pliny the Elder described how this good was created through salting and boiling in large lead vats that resulted in a terrible odor. The dibapha variety of this good featured prominently on the (*) togas of Roman senators. The production of one pound of this good required the deaths of 10,000 animals of the genus Murex. For 10 points, name this Phoenician good produced from the fluid of crushed snails.
2.r: Tyrian purple [accept purple dye and other equivalents; prompt on Murex snails with “what comes from the snails?”]

2.q: Israeli historian Yuri Pines analyzes the trend of thought towards "the people" during this period in his work Envisioning Eternal Empire. Coins described as either "ghost-faced" or "ant-nosed" were likely first produced during this period. A ruler who took the title of "August Thearch" following this period was the son of a concubine and the merchant "Master Lu". According to one source, the general (*) Bai Qi ("bye chee") decapitated 240,000 soldiers at a battle during this period. Historians consider the Partition of Jin as marking the shift from the Spring and Autumn period to this one. The maxim "If you know both yourself and your enemy, you can win one hundred battles" is derived from a treatise written during this period, Sun Tzu's Art of War. For 10 points, name this period which ended with Qin's conquest of China.
2.r: Warring States period [or Zhànguó Shídài; do not accept or prompt on "Sengoku Jidai" as that almost always refers to the much later one in Japan]

2.q: Soil salinization led to this crop being favoured over the similar zizzu around the start of the ED 1 period. A controversial hypothesis, which argues that this crop's use for non-nutritional purposes at sites like Raqefet Cave preceded its use for food, is supported by Edward Seligman. This crop was the main ingredient in a recipe found in the Hymn to Ninkasi written by a culture that used it as a currency. This crop was paired with the similar species of (*) emmer and einkorn in the so-called "Neolithic package", which was grown at sites like Catalhoyuk before becoming the main crop of city states like Nippur and Eridu. For 10 points, the first farmers of the Fertile Crescent relied on the cereal crops rye, wheat, and what other crop used to make ancient beer?
2.r: barley [or Hordeum vulgare; accept Hordeum vulgare spontaneum; accept se or seum; prompt on grain; prompt on cereal until mentioned; prompt on wheat until read and ask “what other, similar crop was used?”]

2.q: Georgina Herrmann proposed that early routes for this material's trade ran through the work site at Tepe Hissar ("TEP-ay HISS-arr"), where artifacts made of this material and alabaster were found. The Harappan colony of Shortugai was founded to acquire this material. This material is found in the eyes of the iconic statue of Ebih II ("EB-ee the second") of Mari and decorates the background of the Standard of Ur. For several millennia, this material has been mined at Sar-i Sang in the Badakhshan province of (*) Afghanistan. This mineral, turquoise, and gold were used to decorate the exteriors of Tutankhamun's funeral mask; it also decorates most of the Ishtar Gate. In the Renaissance, this mineral was ground to make the extremely expensive pigment ultramarine. For 10 points, name this valuable stone historically used for blue dyes.

Benedict Anderson adopted a title originally used by leaders on this body of water to refer to Filipino semi-feudalistic society. Theodore de Bry made many engravings for an author who advocated for people on this body of water and was welcomed by the queen Anacaona. After failing to convince others to perform a dance called an areito, a revolt on this body of water was led by Hatuey. A branch of people indigenous to this body of water, the (*) Lucayan, were nearly extinct prior to a visit to this body of water by Bartolome de las Casas. The Taino were the indigenous people of, for 10 points, what body of water where Christopher Columbus arrived at the Bahamas?

This country allowed the visiting 1981 Springbok Tour to take place in violation of its obligations under the Gleneagles Agreement. The French government conducted Operation Satanique in this country. Fernando Pereira died when the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior sank off the coast of this country. The introduction of European weapons to this country triggered the (*) Musket Wars here, which were followed by the Land Wars. In 1893, this country became the first in the world to grant women the right to vote. This country's Indigenous people signed the Treaty of Waitangi with the British. For 10 points each, name this country home to the Maori people.

To regulate water use, a kingdom based in this region constructed five wewas for an artificial "sea" dated to the 4th century CE. This region's holiday of Poson commemorates a meeting between King Tissa and Mahinda. The first kingdom of an ethnic group from this region was named for the copper sand that stained its founder's hands upon his arrival; that founder was Prince (*) Vijaya. Attendees of a non-Sarvastivada "Fourth Council" held in this region transcribed the Tripitaka onto palm leaves. Per the Mahavamsa, this region was home to a mythical fort ruled by the demon king Ravana. This region's Kingdom of Anuradhapura fell following invasions by the Chola Empire to the north. For 10 points, name this Buddhist-majority island country primarily inhabited by the Sinhalese.
2.r: Sri Lanka [or Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka or Śrī Laṅkā Prajātāntrika Samājavādī Janarajaya or Ilaṅgai Jaṉanāyaka Sōsalisak Kuḍiyarasu; accept Lanka; accept Ceylon] (The unmentioned kingdoms in the first and third lines are the Kingdoms of Polonnaruwa and Tambapaṇṇī.)

2.q: The Avro Arrow was a planned supersonic fighter jet for this country's air force. The Sikh extremist group Babbar Khalsa bombed Air India Flight 182 as it left this country. Bombardier is an airplane manufacturer in this country, whose aforementioned Avro Arrow was cancelled by prime minister John (*) Diefenbaker. This country launched Operation Yellow Ribbon to handle a flux of diverted flights, with many of the stranded passengers being housed in towns like Gander in Newfoundland and Labrador. For 10 points, name this country that grounded several flights while their southern neighbor experienced the 9/11 attacks.

Rulers with this title employed a series of lash-bearers to patrol the streets while ruling a city where they stripped voting rights from everyone except a group called "the Included." After overthrowing the Bacchiadae, Cypselos took this title, as did his son Periander. Harmodius and Aristogeiton planned an attack targeted a ruler with this title at the 514 BC Panathenaic Festival, where they killed Hipparchus but failed to kill the final holder in a line of rulers who took this title, Hippias. (*) Thrasybulus led a 403 BC uprising to overthrow a regime whose rulers took this title. That regime whose leaders took this title was imposed on a city after its defeat in the Peloponnesian War. For 10 points, give this title, held by "Thirty" rulers in a pro-Spartan oligarchy that ruled Athens.

Australian general George Vasey famously declared "Here we bloody well are and here we bloody well stay" during a 1941 battle to defend Bralos and this location. A battle fought at this location was the first major engagement of the Roman-Seleucid war and resulted in Antiochus III being forced to flee Greece. A memorial stone at this location bears an inscription encouraging the reader to (*) "go tell the Spartans" that "we lie here, obedient to their words". Upon being told to surrender his arms at this location, one military leader issued the famous retort "Molon labe", or "come and take them.'' A battle at this location took place simultaneously with a naval battle at Artemisium. For 10 points, name this location where Leonidas led a defending force of three hundred Spartans against the Persians.

After this resource's indiscriminate harvesting was made illegal in the Lacey Act, Guy Bradley was killed trying to prevent illegal collection of it. Kalaniʻopuʻu ("kah-LA-nee-yo-POO-oo") gifted several ʻAhu ʻula, which are primarily made of this resource, to Captain Cook shortly before Cook was killed. Xokonoschtletl ("SHOW-koh-noh-SHLEH-tul") Gomora has led a campaign to return a massive object made of this material named for Moctezuma II. While walking in New York City, Frank Chapman noted the large number of (*) hats made from this material. Scalping, capturing horses, and taking prisoners are some of the required tasks to decorate a war bonnet with this material. Many Great Plains Native American headdresses are made from, for 10 points, what material that is harvested from birds?

Mike Harcourt failed to protect residents of this city from evictions in the leadup to an event with the theme "Transportation and Communication: World in Motion - World in Touch." That event led to the coining of the term SkyTrain for this city's public transit system. The Asiatic Exclusion League led a series of 1907 Anti-Oriental Riots in this city, in which demonstrators advocating for indigenous women tore down the statue of an ex-prospector who founded this city's (*) Gastown neighborhood following the Cariboo Gold Rush. This city hosted the 1986 World's Fair, and the Sea to Sky highway connects it to Whistler, where the ski events of the 2010 Winter Olympics took place. For 10 points, name this large city on Canada's Western shore, the most populous in British Columbia.

This policy in Canada led to a boom in the economy of the French fishing islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon. Prince Edward Island notably had this policy for almost fifty years starting in 1901, while Quebec repealed it after less than a year. The fact that this policy in Ontario did not include manufacturing for export allowed Hamilton's Rocco Perri to profit from (*) border crossings at Windsor. Canadian adoption of this policy was advocated by local branches of an organization founded by Frances Willard supported by Canadian suffragists, the WCTU. For 10 points, name this policy which led to a boom in organized crime in Canada during the 1920s, introduced by the Eighteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.
2.r: prohibition of alcohol [accept temperance; accept banning alcohol or other descriptions such as prohibiting alcohol]

2.q: According to Plutarch, this man pretended to have diarrhea as an excuse to reveal Saturninus' political plans to his rivals. This leader scandalized the Senate by presiding over it while wearing triumphal robes instead of a toga after a conflict in which his subordinate made overtures to Bocchus I. Metellus mentored this leader, who eventually fulfilled a prophecy involving (*) eagle chicks. This leader's forces were defeated at the Colline Gate by a rival who ordered several proscriptions. This leader defeated the Cimbri at Vercellae, earning him the moniker "third founder of Rome". This leader defeated Jugurtha and introduced the cohort in his namesake military reforms. For 10 points, name this Roman general and rival of Sulla.

Soldiers fighting in this empire used goatskin bags as flotation devices to cross rivers during campaigns. Hadadezer led a coalition of eleven kings to combat this empire's conquest of Aram. This empire's record of the names of those kings is one of the few extra-biblical mentions of King Ahab. According to Herodotus, the army of this empire was crippled when scores of mice chewed threw their (*) bowstrings. Remnants of this empire's army joined an Egyptian army under Necho II to lay siege to the city of Harran, but ended up being crushed by Nebuchadnezzar at the Battle of Carchemish. Shalmaneser III and Sennacherib were rulers of, for 10 points, which ancient Near Eastern empire with a capital at Nineveh?

King Louis-Philippe tasked Marshal Jean-de-Dieu Soult ("zhawn-day-d'yoo soolt") with quashing a series of revolts among producers of this commodity known as canuts ("can-oots"). Following the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, this commodity began being produced in England after thousands of Huguenots fled to Norwich. Lyon ("lee-ON") was a historical center for production of this commodity in France, and its pioneer Olivier (*) de Serres provided his name to the process of making it. During the reign of Frederick the Great, thousands of mulberry trees were planted across Germany to aid in the production of this good. Produced by the larvae of Bombyx mori worms, for 10 points, name this luxurious fiber, whose namesake "Road" consisted of trade routes connecting Europe with Asia.
2.c: 2019 Florida Spring Tournament (FST) Pkt H. Packet 8 Q23

2.q: This ruler's forces legendarily won a battle after a mule's birth inspired Zopyrus to injure himself to trick an enemy. This ruler executed the nobleman Intaphernes, who had helped bring him to power. In an artwork commissioned by this ruler, he steps on the head of Bardiya, who he claimed was a mage named Gaumata. The Battle of Lade occurred during a revolt against this ruler quashed by his commander Datis. The (*) Behistun Inscription was commissioned by this ruler, whose troops quashed the Ionian Revolt. This ruler's troops were defeated by Miltiades' Athenian forces at the Battle of Marathon. For 10 points, name this Achaemenid emperor and father of Xerxes the Great.

This historian wrote that people "only regard each other as useful objects," in the manner of another author's book The Ego and Its Own, in a passage examining St. Giles and other neighborhoods in "great towns." This historian used Wilhelm Zimmerman's data as a source for his monograph The Peasant War in Germany. At the request of Paul Lafargue ("luh-FARG"), this historian excerpted three chapters from one of his polemics in a pamphlet that examines "utopian and scientific" forms of the title ideology. This author's book attacking (*) Eugen Duhring ("OY-gen DUE-ring") introduced his idea that the state would "wither away over time." While in Manchester during the 1840s, this dialectical materialist collected statistics about local laborers for his book The Condition of the Working Class in England. For 10 points, name this man who, with Karl Marx, co-wrote The Communist Manifesto.

The son of an exiled Jewish princess mythically became the ruler of this empire after suggesting that its crown be placed between two lions. A prince of this empire fled to the Tang Dynasty after a treacherous miller killed his father. A ruler of this empire reigned for 70 years after he was legendarily crowned within his mother's womb. Mani dedicated his only major non-Syriac work to a ruler of this empire, but was later executed by its ruler (*) Bahram I. A ruler of this empire who signed a treaty of "perpetual peace" finished the compilation of the "Great Avesta." The Roman emperor Valerian was used as a step stool by this empire's ruler Shapur I. For 10 points, name this last Zoroastrian Persian Empire, which succeeded the Parthians.

This site's "Thousand-Year Gap" was solved by Wilhelm Dorpfield after successfully dating pottery and finding a weaker section of this site's wall. A conflict near this site between a people known as the Wilusa and raiders called the Ahhiyawa is recorded on tablets found in (*) Hattusas. This site's sixth and seventh iterations were rapidly destroyed in the late Bronze Age, possibly due to an earthquake or fire. This site was first excavated by amatuer archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann while visiting a friend's land in Northwestern Turkey. For 10 points, name this archaeological site theorized to be the setting of the Homeric epic The Iliad.

[NOTE TO PLAYERS (to be read aloud): description acceptable.] In one rebellion led by members of this non-Irish group, a battle known as its country's "Battle of Vinegar Hill" was lost by insurrectionaries who proclaimed "Death or Liberty." One member of this group, James Ruse, developed an early successful farm known as Experiment farm. Before the arrival of the French La Recherche and L'Esperance, many members of this group got sick and died due to hard labor imposed on them by Captain Arthur (*) Philip. The Blue Mountains halted the progress of this group until a passage over the mountains was discovered. Some members of this group were transported aboard the HMS Supply and reached Botany Bay in 1787. For 10 points, identify this group primarily consisting of convicts who settled the colony of New South Wales.
2.r: convicts transported to Australia [accept equivalents that indicated that they were Europeans who settled Australia; prompt on answers ike British convicts]

2.q: A quartzite shrine built by this ruler, the Red Chapel, was reassembled by Henri Chevrier and Pierre Lacau. This ruler held a heb sed jubilee after fifteen years on the throne rather than the traditional thirty years. This ruler lavished over 90 titles onto the commoner Senenmut, who may have designed this ruler's mortuary temple of Djeser-Djeseru. Inscriptions with this ruler's name, which survived a brief campaign of (*) erasure ended by Amenhotep II ("the second"), confused Jean-Francois Champollion until he identified redactions as a royal name. This ruler became a full pharaoh during her coregency with Thutmose III ("the third"), who was both her stepson and nephew. For 10 points, name this New Kingdom pharaoh, the first and longest reigning woman to rule ancient Egypt.

In this region, the Tunnug 1 burial mound containing men and horses placed atop a dead ruler may corroborate Herodotus's description of "spectral riders." Ivory Venus figurines with hooded and striped features were found at a village in this region linked to the Upper Paleolithic Mal'ta-Buret' culture. A complex in this region contains one of the earliest known pile carpets and the resting place of a "Maiden" from the Pazyryk culture. Neanderthals may have (*) interbred with a species of hominids named after a cave in this region, the Denisovans. Over ten thousand years ago, humans may have crossed from this region into North America using the Bering land bridge. For 10 points, woolly rhinoceroses once roamed what cold, expansive region of Russia?
2.r: Siberia [prompt on Tuva or Mongolia or Altai Mountains or Chukchi Peninsula by asking “what larger region is it part of?”; prompt on Northern Russia or Asia or Eurasia by asking “what more specific region?”]

2.q: Camilla Towsend used newly translated sources on this empire, often written by women, in a 2019 revisionist New History. Internal affairs in this empire were managed by people with a deceptive title meaning "female snake," who were male and often related to its "great speakers." Schools and farmlands in this empire were organized in districts called calpulli. This empire fought nearby city-states like (*) Cholula in short, ritualized wars with preselected times for battles intended to take captives. This empire succeeded the rule of Tepanec as an informal "Triple Alliance" ruled equally between three altepetl city-states, but came to be dominated by a city on Lake Texcoco. For 10 points, name this empire that ruled over the Valley of Mexico from the city of Tenochtitlan.
2.r: Aztec Empire [accept the Mexica, accept the Triple Alliance until read]

2.q: Journalist Marie Colvin wore an eyepatch after being injured during a war on this island. The Black July pogroms targeted a rebel group on this island who attempted to establish an independent state named Eelam. (EE-rum). An inland kingdom on this island centered on the city of Kandy(CON-dee) repelled numerous invasions by Portuguese and Dutch colonists. A decades-long civil war on this island was fought between its majority (*) Sinhalese people and the separatist Tamil Tigers. Ceylon was the former name of this island, which is governed from Colombo. For 10 points, name this island country off the southeast coast of India.
2.r: Sri Lanka [or Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka, accept Ceylon before mention]

2.q: Following this man's most notable undertaking, he was sent on a diplomatic mission to persuade Argentina to enter World War I. John Rowett helped fund one of this man's expeditions. Frank Hurley documented one of this explorer's expeditions using an early form of color photography. Along with Tom Crean and Frank Worsley, this explorer crossed a certain island with only 50 feet of rope and an adze ("ads"). This explorer climbed Mount (*) Erebus during his Nimrod expedition. This man and five crew members rowed 800 miles in a lifeboat after being shipwrecked, eventually drifting to Elephant Island. The ill-fated Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition was led by, for 10 points, what British Antarctic explorer who commanded the HMS Endurance?

Hundreds in this country developed Onsan Illness as a result of its Heavy-Chemical Industry Drive. The Hanbo Scandal in this country contributed to the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis. This non-island country is one of the Four Asian Tigers. The rapid economic growth of this country starting in the 1960's was called the Miracle on the (*) Han River. Numerous "chaebol" conglomerates wield large political power in this country. In 2004, the "Digital City" office park was built by this country's largest company, Samsung. For 10 points, name this country governed from Seoul.

A bronze miniature of one of these objects found at Daimabad is among the miniature examples found at Harappan sites, which lack practical full-size examples that may have been found in modern India at Sinauli. The use of these objects, distinguished in the Rig Veda from anas, is linked to the settlement of South Asia by the Indo-Aryans. Before the Battle of Hydaspes, the Macedonian cavalry completely routed users of these objects under the younger Porus thanks to heavy (*) rains that fell the night before. These objects, called ratha in India, had a "scythed" form used by Achaemenid Persia to counter heavy infantry. Though elephants and horse archers replaced these Bronze Age objects in Indian warfare, they remained a status symbol partly due to their association with Krishna in the Mahabharata. For 10 points, name these wheeled vehicles used in ancient warfare.

A speech given by this leader against one national referendum warned that it would create "six categories" of citizens in his country. This leader sympathized with miners during the editing of a book on the Asbestos Strike of 1949. As his country's Minister of Justice, this leader defended decriminalizing homosexuality by claiming there was "no place for the state in the (*) bedrooms of the nation." This leader fully ended British authority over his country by enacting the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. After the kidnapping of James Cross and Pierre LaPorte, this leader declared "Just watch me" before invoking the War Measures Act. For 10 points, name this Canadian Prime Minister, the father of current Canadian Prime Minister Justin.
2.r: Pierre Trudeau [accept Joseph Philippe Pierre Yves Elliott Trudeau; prompt on Trudeau]

2.q: As minister of justice, this person ordered the execution of the crowd-drawing Shaozheng Mao for the crime of perverted speech. Empress Dowager Dou resisted this person's influence on her grandson's Jianyuan reforms. This statesman led a campaign to tear down the walls of three noble families in his home state of Lu. This man supposedly compiled the Book of Documents and the (*) Spring and Autumn Annals, which Li Si ordered destroyed. Sima Qian may have lied about hundreds of this man's followers being buried alive under Qin Shi Huang. Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty made this man's Five Classics the basis of official state ideology. For 10 points, name this philosopher whose Analects informed imperial governance.

Records of this ruler's navy were collected on the Anthony Roll and include warships such as the Antelope and Salamander. This author of the anti-Lutheran tract Assertio septem sacramentorum abolished the collection of Peter's Pence. After the passage of the Suppression Acts, this monarch faced domestic rebellion led by Robert Aske in the Pilgrimage of (*) Grace, which was in response to this ruler's dissolution of his country's monasteries. This was the highest-ranked person excommunicated by Pope Clement VII as a result of this ruler's Act of Supremacy and his subsequent divorce and remarriage to Anne Boleyn. For 10 points, name this king of the Tudor dynasty who founded the Church of England as part of a dispute over his six wives.

This empire's deliberative body was the "Great Assembly," whose first meeting had 29 clans presided over by a belen-tigui, or master of ceremony. This empire's first ruler did not walk until he was seven years old, according to a history that was recounted orally by griots. The founder of this empire defeated the Sosso ruler Sumanguru at the Battle of Kirina. This empire was founded by (*) Sundiata, and a later ruler of this empire devalued gold all along his route during his hajj to Mecca. For 10 points, name this West African empire that was ruled by Mansa Musa, which shares its name with a modern-day country.
2.r: Mali [or the Mali Empire; or the Malinke Empire; or the Mandingo Empire]

2.q: A woman who performed this activity is depicted in a ceramic figurine that doubles as a whistle from Jaina Island. Instances of this practice are thought to have begun with the usage of a tool called a manopla. Sculptures called hacha were inspired by this practice, from which the modern ollama is descended. Heavy yoke belts were used for this practice, which required stone (*) rings installed on facilities for it. I-shaped courts in cities like Tikal were used for this practice, whose central object was struck with the hips and thighs of teams of two to three men. For 10 points, name this ritual sport played by several Mesoamerican civilizations with a namesake round rubber object.
2.r: Mesoamerican ball game [or ollamaliztli; or pitz; accept juego de pelota mesoamericano; accept juego de pelota maya]

2.q: This region, known by ancient denizens as the "Mining Country," may have received its modern name from a god who rode a winged bull and had a beard made of lapis lazuli. Pompey was murdered in one city in this region while a waterway built by Necho was later converted into "Trajan's River." In modern history, this region was the target of of Operation (*) Badr to seize the Bar Lev Line, occurring simultaneously with an other Islamic nation's attempt to conquer the Golan Heights during the Yom Kippur War. Anwar Sadat allowed another nation to traverse this peninsula navally through a canal after signing its namesake "Disengagement Act."For 10 points, name this peninsula that acts as a land bridge between Africa and Asia in the nation of Egypt.
2.c: 2018 Florida Spring Tournament (FST) Pkt I. Packet 9 Q17

2.q: An early form of pottery in this region was the glossy 'ripple ware' of the Badarian Culture. A catfish and a chisel in a serekh represented the name of a king who ruled parts of this region during its Naqada III phase. That king, who may have ruled this region's undiscovered city of Thinis, was called Min by Herodotus. A siltstone tablet shows a ruler of this region holding an enemy's (*) hair and preparing to smite him. An accessory known in Greek as the Pschent represented this region's unity by combining a red vulture crown and a white cobra crown. The reign of a king named Menes or Narmer marks the end of this region's Predynastic period. For 10 points, name this region whose "Lower" and "Upper" divisions were united by the first Pharaohs.
2.r: Ancient Egypt [or anything with the consonants kmt; or Upper Egypt; or Lower Egypt; prompt on North Africa]

2.q: A ruler of this region sent a bundle of golden arrows to Rome, saying "if you want war, keep the arrows, because you are going to need them." During the 3rd century CE, the Wayekiye ["way-ya-kee-yah"] priests ruled the northern part of this region, a mining center called the Land of Thirty Schoinoi ["sco-in-oi"]. Strabo describes a "fierce one-eyed queen" of this region named Amanirenas ["a-man-nee-ray-nass"], who defeated the Romans at Syene [sigh-een]. Gaius Petronius sacked this region's traditional northern capital of (*) Napata. A kingdom of this region, ruled by queens called Kandake, was centered at the capital of Meroe, the site of numerous small pyramids. For 10 points, name this region in modern-day Sudan south of Egypt that was home to the pyramid-building Kingdom of Kush.
2.r: Nubia [or Lower or Higher Nubia; or Kush until mentioned]

2.q: The Roman term for these beings, Luca bos, refers to their appearance at the battle of Heraclea. Surus was the last one of these beings that survived a campaign which had begun with the siege of Saguntum. 500 of these animals were given to Seleucus ("suh-loo-kus") by (*) Chandragupta in exchange for several eastern satrapies. They aren't camels, but carriages called howdahs were historically used when riding these creatures. Some of these animals were frightened by horn blasts, causing Carthage to lose the battle of Zama. For 10 points, name these animals, which Hannibal brought across the Alps during his invasion of Rome.

A history of this empire contains a prophecy declaring the founder of the Massina state to be the Mahdi. Nehemia Levitzion argued that a copy of a history of this empire, dubbed "Manuscript C," was forged by Shehu Amadu. The supposedly 125-year old Mahmud Kati is attributed an account of this empire's history named the Chronicle of the Seeker, or the Tarikh al-fattash. That chronicle was commissioned by this empire's ruler (*) Dawud, who fought over the salt mines of Taghaza with Morocco. The earlier hajj of Mansa Musa was plagarized for the account of the pilgrimage of this empire's ruler Aski Muhammad, the successor of Sonni Ali. For 10 points, name this West African empire, ruled from Gao, which supplanted Mali.

Annual celebrations of this industry occur in its historic Japanese center Taiji. This industry used large metal pots called trywork for the boiling needed for processing. Firsthand accounts of a disaster in this industry by Thomas Nickerson and Owen Chase provided sources for a 2000 Nathaniel Philbrick book. Competition in this industry led to a protracted conflict over the settling of (*) Spitsbergen. Australia has historically been the most vocal opposition to the so-called "scientific" form of this industry used to circumvent a 1982 moratorium. This industry, which powered the economy of 19th-century New Bedford, provided material for Victorian women's corsets and pre-kerosene lamps. For 10 points, name this industry that involves hunting oil-rich marine mammals.

In a design for one of these structures, John Smeaton pioneered the use of hydraulic lime. Multiple influential designs for these structures were constructed around the hazardous Eddystone Rocks near Cornwall. The oldest one of these structures still standing is the Tower of Hercules, which was initially named the Farum Brigantium. The Fresnel ("freh-nell") (*) lens was developed for use in these structures. Ptolemy II ("tall-a-mee the 2nd") commissioned one of these structures in Egypt, which became one of the Seven Wonders. That one of these tall structures on the island of Pharos featured a bright furnace at the top. For 10 points, name these structures that included an ancient one in Alexandria that helped guide ships into port.

One history of this empire was written by the historian Berossus, who described one site in this empire purportedly discovered by Robert Koldewey. One ruler of this empire defeated Zimri-Lim to conquer the kingdom of Mari. Another ruler of this empire enlisted the help of Cyaxares during a war that ended when his successor won the Battle of (*) Carchemish. That successor started this empire's namesake "captivity" after conquering the Kingdom of Judah. A seven-foot-tall stele contains one text written by a ruler of this empire decreeing principles like "an eye for an eye." Nebuchadnezzar and Hammurabi ruled, for 10 points, what empire whose capital was known for its apocryphal hanging gardens?

During the Edo period, people in this profession called hikeshi who wore coats matching their elaborate tattoos were associated with the "autumn flowers" of Edo. Marcus Egnatius Rufus gained fame in Rome by employing 600 men in this profession, which was also the main function of watchmen called vigiles founded by Augustus. Three people of this profession standing at "the Pile" were photographed raising an American flag. A private squad of this profession that would offer to purchase (*) property from ancient Romans was organized by Crassus. People of this profession were unable to prevent a 64 AD event that Nero apocryphally spent playing his fiddle. For 10 points, over 300 people in what profession in New York passed away as first responders during 9/11?
2.r: firefighter [or firemen; accept hikeshi until read; prompt on police or police officer and ask “what other profession was involved in those events?”]

2.q: The Athenian lawgiver Draco had his legislation posted onto examples of these structures called kyrbeis ("keer-bay-ees"). The Aurelian Walls incorporated one of these structures named for Gaius Cestius. The mythological giant Xelhua supposedly built a "Great" one of these structures in Cholula. The Avenue of the Dead linked two large examples of these structures "of the (*) Sun" and "of the Moon" located in Teotihuacan that were often used for human sacrifices. The Saqqara necropolis is home to a "step" example of one of these structures designed by Imhotep as the burial site for Djoser. Giza was home to, for 10 points, what structures that housed the tombs of ancient Egyptian pharaohs?
2.r: pyramids [prompt on tombs or temples with “What type of building were they?”]

2.q: Lucius Aemilius chose this process for two of his sons to help them ascend the cursus honorum. Publius Fonteius helped Publius Clodius Pulcher undergo this process in his controversial bid to become tribune of the plebs. A rare example of this process permitted for women was undertaken posthumously by Augustus for his wife Livia. In 97 AD, terminal illness and a Praetorian Guard revolt forced Emperor (*) Nerva to use this process. Men undergoing this process would usually maintain their original nomen as a cognomen. Marcus Aurelius broke the Five Good Emperors' tradition of succession via this process by selecting Commodus as heir. For 10 points, name this process that allowed Octavian to inherit Julius Caesar's fortune and was often used to maintain Roman family lines.
2.r: adoption [or adoptio or adoptatio; accept adoption to become a pleb; prompt answers describing becoming a plebeian and ask how that was accomplished]

2.q: The 1842 Great Fire of Hamburg prompted the construction of the first modern one of these structures in continental Europe, which was designed by William Lindley. Ellis Chesbrough designed one of these structures in Chicago by raising the city four feet, the first comprehensive one of its kind in the U.S. Edwin Chadwick oversaw the creation of one of these structures designed by Joseph (*) Bazalgette, who constructed the Victoria and Chelsea Embankments as part of them. That one of these structures was built in London due to the Great Stink of 1858. Tarquin the Elder apocryphally constructed one of these structures in Rome called the Cloaca Maxima, which drained into the Tiber. For 10 points, name these sanitary structures that dispose of waste.
2.r: sewer systems [accept sewage systems or drainage systems or wastewater treatment systems]

2.q: A material culture named for these objects made sickle-shaped marks that are interpreted as numerals, was succeeded by the Halstatt ("HALL-shtott") culture, and thrived in Central Europe until the mid-8th century BC. Romans placed these objects in niches inside of buildings whose name comes from the Latin word for "dove." They're not for holding wine or oil, but the elaborate Derveni krater was used as one of these objects. The use of lekythoi and (*) amphorae as cinerary ("SIN-er-AIR-ee") examples of these objects declined as inhumation became more common. The mid-17th-century discovery of several of these objects in Norfolk inspired an essay by Sir Thomas Browne. These objects, which are common grave goods, are displayed in a columbarium. For 10 points, identify these vessels that hold funerary ashes.
2.r: urns [accept burial urns; prompt on vases or pottery or amphorae or krater or jars; accept Urnfield Culture or Hydriotaphia, Urn Burial; prompt on busts by asking “what is the bust placed alongside in the niche?”] (The word for “dove” is columba, so columbarium means “dovecote.”)

2.q: This emperor sacked the influential freedman Pallas from the treasury in the second year of his namesake quinquennium. Aelius Aristides claimed this emperor planned a canal through the Isthmus of Corinth, a project he ceremonially inaugurated but never completed. Troops loyal to this emperor put down a rebellion led by disgruntled governor Gaius Julius Vindex. After the destruction of his first residence, the (*) Domus Transitoria, this emperor built a palace complex named after its extensive use of gold leaf, the Domus Aurea. This emperor likely orchestrated the deaths of Britannicus and his mother Agrippina the Younger before dying by suicide in AD 68. For 10 points, name this final Julio-Claudian emperor who supposedly played the fiddle during the Great Fire of Rome.
2.r: Nero [or Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus or Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus]

2.q: A regiment from this island was wiped out at Beaumont Hamel on the first day of the Battle of the Somme. Shanawdithit was the last known member of this island's extinct Indigenous population, the Beothuks. European explorers built the settlement of (*) L'Anse aux Meadows on this island, providing archaeological evidence for a land known as Vinland. This island's traditional cod fishery off the Grand Banks collapsed in the 1990s. Joey Smallwood is sometimes called the last Father of Confederation for leading this island into Confederation. For 10 points, name this province that joined Canada in 1949 alongside Labrador.
2.r: Newfoundland [accept Newfoundland and Labrador or Dominion of Newfoundland; prompt on NL]

2.q: An island off the coast of this modern-day country was where the HMS Wager shipwrecked, as described in a 2023 David Grann book about its subsequent mutiny. In this country, indigenous groups like the Chono and Kawesqar spent most of their time in large canoes containing permanent fires. Thomas Cochrane left Britain in disgrace to command this country's navy, where he led an expedition to take a colonial fort founded by Pedro de (*) Valdivia. Alexander Selkirk allegedly inspired Robinson Crusoe by spending four years as a castaway on this country's Juan Fernandez Islands. In 1888, this country annexed an island whose indigenous people created the rongorongo glyph system and moai statues. For 10 points, what South American country administers Easter Island?
2.r: Republic of Chile [accept the General Captaincy of Chile, Governorate of Chile, or Kingdom of Chile]

2.q: In 1981, this region passed a law banning women from taking their husband's surname upon marriage. Five people were killed in anti-conscription riots in this region during Easter 1918, but the government of Robert Borden imposed it anyway. This province underwent a period of rapid liberalisation called the "Quiet Revolution" following the conservative rule of long-term Premier (*) Maurice Duplessis. "Money and the ethnic vote" were blamed for the failure of an independence referendum in this province. After the FLQ kidnapped two government officials in this province, Pierre Trudeau invoked the War Measures Act. For 10 points, name this only majority French-speaking Canadian province.

Wealth from this commodity allowed the Czech city of Kutna Hora to compete with Prague for importance by supplying material for groschen. It's not a food, but this was the main commodity whose decline in production led to a 15th-century "Great Famine." Material used to process this commodity produced by indigenous labor in Huancavelica replaced European sources at Almaden. During the height of the Spanish Empire, this was the main commodity shipped west from (*) Acapulco to exchange for Chinese silk and porcelain on the Manila Galleons. This was the less valuable of two commodities whose extraction at Potosi for specie would lead to massive inflation in the Spanish Empire. For 10 points, name this commodity that was used to make the "piece of eight," or the Spanish dollar.
2.r: silver [prompt on bullion, prompt on mercury by asking “what other commodity was it used to process?”]

2.q: Before they were sacked by the Normans, the cities of Corinth and Thebes were centers for the production of this good in the Byzantine Empire. The arrival of Huguenot refugees precipitated the production of this good in the London district of Spitalfields. The canuts of Lyon processed this good using a programmable machine invented by Joseph Marie Jacquard. One monopoly on this good's production was ended after two Nestorian (*) monks smuggled it on behalf of Justinian. This good's production apocryphally began under Empress Leizu in ancient China and relied on mulberry leaves. For 10 points, name this fabric produced from a certain insect that also names a trade route which connected Europe and the Far East.

A clerical leader that worked in this city denounced Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus. This city was home to the largest Jewish population in antiquity and was where the Septuagint ("SEP-tew-a-jint") was compiled. The Heptastation causeway connected this city to the island of Pharos. A pagan mathematician that worked in this city was murdered by a mob of Christians; that female mathematician was (*) Hypatia. This city's serapeum was destroyed on the orders of Theophilus. Ptolemy I Soter moved his capital from Memphis to this city. A lighthouse in this city was considered to be one of the Wonders of the World. For 10 points, name this Egyptian city, home to a famous library.

The battle of Lugalo was fought against this empire's forces by a leader whose skull was identified by Edward Twining by the presence of a bullet hole. Mkwawa resisted this empire in a territory that was damaged by the Abushiri revolt. Samuel Maharero was defeated by this country's forces at the Battle of Waterberg, leading to the opening of a concentration camp on Shark Island. A person styled Bokero who promised that bullets would turn to water resisted this empire in the (*) Maji Maji rebellion.The gunboat Panther was deployed by this country, kicking off the Agadir Crisis. The genocide of the Herero and Namaqua were committed by this country's forces, who controlled much of Togo, Namibia, and Cameroon. For 10 points, name this country that colonized much of Africa under Kaiser Wilhelm II.

A major hub for these people was founded by exiles from Hornacheros in an old quarter on the Bou Regreg river. The activities of one of these people, the Englishman Jack Ward, nearly triggered a war between Venice and England. A community of these people, which included expelled Moriscos, elected Jan Janszoon to lead the semi-independent Republic of Sale. Before entering the service of the Ottoman state, (*) Hayreddin Barbarossa was one of these people who battled the Spanish. The first overseas deployment of the United States Marine Corps was during a series of wars against these people after Thomas Jefferson refused to meet their demands for tribute. For 10 points, name these seafaring marauders who harassed Mediterranean trade from ports such as Tunis and Algiers.
2.r: Barbary pirates [or Barbary corsairs or Barbary privateers; accept Ottoman pirates or Ottoman corsairs or Ottoman privateers until “Ottoman” is read; prompt on pirates or corsairs or privateers]

2.q: According to Antiochus of Syracuse, the first of these people were chosen from men who didn't fight in the Messenian war, while children were designated Partheniae. Brasidas recruited a unit of these people dubbed the "new to the demos." Pollux claimed these people surpassed douloi and oiketai in power. According to Thucydides, 2,000 of these people were executed in the wake of an earthquake at Cape Taenarus. These people were the target of an annual declaration of (*) war by elected Ephors, who would pardon their killers from miasma. During the krypteia, these people's dogskin caps designated them targets for murder as part of the agoge (a-go-jay). Messenia and Southern Laconia were the most common homelands for these people, who could serve as a hoplite or pay 500 drachmae for their freedom. For 10 points, name this servile class of Sparta.

Allegedly, this man might have been the bastard child of Lucy Montagu and Prince Frederick Lewis. This leader succeeded to the office of Chancellor of the Exchequer upon the sudden death of Charles Townshend. This man served as Secretary of State for the Home Department in a coalition ministry with Charles (*) Fox. After Robert Walpole, this leader was the first forced out of office for failing a vote of no confidence. Civil unrest during this man's tenure included the anti-Catholic Gordon Riots and insurrection in the colonies following the Intolerable Acts. For 10 points, name this Prime Minister whose government managed the response to the American Revolution.
2.r: Frederick North, Lord North [or Frederick North, 2nd Earl of Guilford]

2.q: The evolution of hereditary kingship among this region's peoples is examined in a book that puts forth "Newton's third law of empires" by Peter Heather. Those peoples of this region were divided into Ingaevones ("ing-eye-WO-nays"), Herminones ("hair-mih-NO-nays"), and Istaevones ("ist-eye-WO-nays") by a classical author who described how a reputation as "lazy fools" had befallen the Cherusci ("khair-OO-skee"). An emperor supposedly bashed his head against the palace walls at night after a (*) defeat in this region, wailing "Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!" This region titles an ethnography by Tacitus, who numbered the Marcomanni and Lombards among its peoples, and, like most Romans, roughly defined it as being north of the Danube and east of the Rhine. For 10 points, name this region where many Romans were slain at the Battle of Teutoburg Forest.

A bombmaker for this organization was nicknamed "the Engineer" and was assassinated when the director of Shin Bet remotely detonated a phone while he was talking to his father. A leader of this group proposed a ten-year truce, or hudna, with its main opponent; that leader of this group, al-Rantissi, was later killed in a targeted air strike. This group often competes with a rival political group founded by Yasser Arafat, which is called Fatah. This group was founded shortly after the start of the First (*) Intifada as an offshoot of Egypt's Muslim Brotherhood. The Al-Qassam Brigades, the military wing of this group, were targeted in 2008 by Operation Cast Lead, an Israeli defense effort. For 10 points, name this Palestinian group that governs the Gaza strip.

A book by Oxford historian Stephanie Dalley posits that this location was actually hundreds of miles to the north of where it is traditionally placed. Berossus is the earliest historical source to mention this location, which was built in his original hometown. Sources frequently named this location after Queen Semiramis ("seh-MEER-uh-miss"), who actually lived at least 200 years before its construction. According to Strabo, an early version of Archimedes' (*) Screw was built for use at this location. Archaeologists have yet to find this place, whose name refers to the trees that drooped over its terraces. The Chaldean ("cal-DEE-in") king Nebuchadnezzar II built this location, which was among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. For 10 points, name this legendary green space in Babylon.

Two answers required. These two rulers met in battle after one traversed the Pass of Jonah and the other executed wounded men left behind at a city on the Pinarus River. During a battle between these two rulers, javelin throwing Agriane skirmishers disrupted a charge of scythed chariots that had been prepared by clearing the battlefield of vegetation. The rebellious Bessus killed one of these rulers and spent a year resisting the other before his execution in (*) Ecbatana. One of these rulers lost courage and fled in two battles after the other led a direct attack with the Companions. The city of Persepolis was burned after these two rulers fought the decisive battles of Issus and Gaugamela. For 10 points, name these two rulers, the last Achaemenid king of Persia and the Macedonian who defeated him.
2.r: Alexander the Great and Darius III [or Alexander III of Macedon and Darayavas III or Dareios III; prompt on Alexander and Darius]

2.q: This politician faced a scandal after it was revealed that members of his predecessor's government had slept with an East German prostitute, Gerda Munsinger. He appointed a group nicknamed the Three Doves, or the Three Wise Men, to his cabinet. Walter Butler proposed an unpopular budget during the "60 days of decision" called for by this man, who removed tariffs on US cars via the Auto Pact. This politician claimed (*) "Canadians do not need to be liberated" in response to the "Vive le Quebec Libre" speech another man gave at Expo 67. This successor of John Diefenbaker appointed a commission that selected the Maple Leaf Flag and won a Nobel Peace Prize for his role in ending the Suez Crisis. For 10 points, name this Liberal Canadian Prime Minister succeeded by Pierre Trudeau.
2.c: 2015 STIMPY Pkt 11. WUSTL A - Ottawa Q11

2.q: To promote this food item, Antoine Parmentier would post guards around his garden, then instruct the guards to accept any bribes from peasants and allow them to be stolen. Following European contact, the Maori replaced their kumara plants with these food items. The American colonies first received these food items in a shipment from Nathaniel Butler, the Governor of Bermuda. People who fled a (*) disaster caused by lack of this food item travelled in "coffin ships." A famine caused by a blight on this food item was alleviated after Robert Peel repealed the "Corn Laws." For 10 points, name this food item that was responsible for a great famine during the 1840s in Ireland.

A kleroterion and bronze pinakion plaques were used to select participants for these events. Public examples of these events, or graphai, were decided by dikastai. Water clocks regulated turn-taking during these events, which often began with a preliminary action known as the anakrisis. The term "sycophant" originally targeted people who repeatedly used these events for monetary gain. Logographers such as the orators (*) Lysias and Demosthenes began their careers by being hired to write speeches specifically for these events, which were often held on the Areopagus. During one of these events that took place at the Eliaia, a philosopher was accused of impiety and corrupting the youth. For 10 points, at what type of event was Socrates sentenced to death by a jury?
2.r: trials [accept court sessions; accept court cases; accept lawsuits; accept being on a jury until read; prompt on speeches or orations by asking “at what events?”; reject “ostracism”]

2.q: The last remnants of this empire's forces were destroyed fighting alongside Necho II, an ally of this empire, at the Battle of Carchemish. A short-lived capital of this empire was Dur-Sharrukin. The deeds of Shalmaneser III were depicted on a Black Obelisk in a later capital of this empire, (*) Nimrud. Buildings from this empire often featured sculptures of winged lion-men, or lamassu. Major rulers of this empire included Tiglath-Pilesar III and Sennacherib. This empire's capital was home to the Library of Ashurbanipal. In 612 BC, a Babylonian-Median coalition sacked this empire's capital, Nineveh. For 10 points, name this Mesopotamian empire, originally governed from Assur.

This island's Eagle Stone features such motifs as the mirror and comb and triple disc. The Tribal Hidage details the presence of kingdoms like Elmet on this island. Pieces of ceremonial weapons found in rivers on this island include a shield showing a boar with elongated legs, and this island was the center of the Arras culture. A helmet from this island shows dancing warriors with crossed wrists and has its eyebrows formed by a gilded dragon. This is the largest island where La Tene culture was present and where (*) Raedwald was likely buried with a ship. The Iceni was one Celtic tribe from here, while the Picts were found in the north of this island. Sutton Hoo contains artifacts from, for 10 points, what island that was conquered by the Anglo-Saxons?

In a divination ceremony from this natural region, a completely black or white animal was sacrificed with a tumi and cremated. According to one source, animals raised in this region were attended by a lower class michi and a supervising camayo. The Chavin people raised an animal in this region to make ch'arky, inspiring the English word jerky. Cavies in this region were likely domesticated to become animals called (*) cuy. The Guinea pig was first domesticated in this natural region and commonly features in the art of the Moche culture. This region's people were the first to domesticate quinoa and potatoes. Wool or cotton was used in this region to make knotted quipus. For 10 points, name this natural region where the alpaca and llama were first domesticated.
2.r: Andes Mountains [accept Andean region; accept the coast of Peru or Mosna Valley; accept Central or Northern Peru; prompt on South America or Western South America]

2.q: During this war, Julia Grace Wales attempted to gather intellectuals to find peace in the Wisconsin Plan. During this war, Hamilton Gault personally funded the creation of a unit whose banner was designed by its colonel and chief and namesake, Princess Patricia. A trowel combined with shield was invented during this war by Sam Hughes, who later feuded over stolen valor with Arthur Currie. Riots on Easter Monday were caused during this war by a policy opposed by Henri (*) Bourassa, during which Julian Byng first rose to prominence. This war, during which Canada first instituted the draft, saw fighting at Passchendaele and Vimy. Canada was led by Robert Borden during, for 10 points, what war during which many Canadians fought at the Somme?

The Mexican newspapers El Hogar and El Excelsior established a holiday dedicated to these people in 1922. Tonantzin was an Aztec goddess who protected these people and was worshiped at a shrine on Tepeyac Hill. Hebe de Bonafini is a long time leader of an organization of these people who are represented by white scarves. Thousands of these people have marched to the (*) Plaza de Mayo since the 1980's to protest desaparecidos from Argentina's Dirty War. The phrase "am I not here, I who am your [this person]" was spoken by a vision to Juan Diego and is inscribed above the Basilica of Guadalupe. The Virgin Mary inspired the "divine" role of, for 10 points, what people who often care for children in Latin American households?
2.r: mothers [prompt on women with “What role do those women have?”]
2.c: 2020 DECAMERON Pkt Applying Strong Sapir-Whorf to Proto-Nostratic Q39

2.q: One of these things in modern-day Nigeria was built in honor of the Ijebu noblewoman Bilikisu Sungbo, although others hypothesize that it was built on the order of the Queen of Sheba. Within the Sindh province of Pakistan, there exists a large one of these objects known as Ranikot that was built by the Talpurs. Construction of Austrian towns characterized by this feature rapidly increased in the 11th century. One of these objects built on the order of Emperor Anastasius (*) stretched from the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara, and was built in Thrace to protect Constantinople from invaders. For 10 points, Qin Shi Huang Di mythically was said to have used bodies in the construction of a "great" object of what type in China?
2.r: walls [accept ditches; accept forts; accept fortifications; accept eredo; prompt on castles, or other terms that indicate large defensive barricades]
2.c: 2019 Florida Spring Tournament (FST) Pkt D. Packet 4 Q23

2.q: Shipwrecks from this war can be seen at very low tides in the pearling village of Broome, which is recounted in Coralie Clarke Rees's elegy Silent His Wings. A riot during this war culminated in the death of Gunner Johnson and the destruction of a post exchange. The perception that foreign troops during this war were "overpaid, oversexed, and over here" culminated in the battle of Brisbane. During this war, (*) "Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels" legendarily carried wounded soldiers along the Kokoda Track. The failure of an expedition to the Klidi Pass during this war prompted the resignation of Prime Minister Robert Menzies. This war's bombing of Darwin was the largest ever attack on Australia; that attack occurred just four days after this war's Battle of Singapore. For 10 points, name this conflict ignited after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor.
2.r: World War II [or Second World War; or Pacific War or Pacific Theater or Asia–Pacific War]

2.q: People seeking to take this action in medieval Japan could serve for three years at the Tokei-ji Temple in Kamakura. After this action was taken against Empress Kassi, civil war broke out in the Mali Empire during the rule of Mansa Suleyman. John Fisher was disgraced and executed after fiercely opposing one of these actions on moral grounds. This action was taken against Pompeia after the Bona Dea affair by (*) Julius Caesar for not being "above suspicion." This action was taken against Eleanor of Aquitaine on the grounds of consanguinity after failing to produce an heir for Louis VII ("the seventh"). For 10 points, name this action that Pope Clement VII refused to allow Henry VIII ("the eighth") to take against Catherine of Aragon, leading to the formation of the Church of England.
2.r: divorces [accept obvious equivalents; accept dissolving a marriage; accept annulment; accept remarriage]

2.q: This civilisation used waterproofed bitumen for one site, which sits across from a 78-room priestly residence known as the "College Hall". A three-headed phallic "Lord of Animals" was found inscribed on an artifact from this civilisation named the Pashupati Seal. Sir Mortimer Wheeler identified one large building at a site from this civilisation as a (*) "Great Granary", located next to a brick-built "Great Bath". One artifact from this civilisation depicts a "dancing girl" with 25 bangles on her left arm."The City of the Cockerel" is a translation of an alternate name of one southern centre of this civilisation, the city of Mohenjo-Daro. For 10 points, identify this civilisation that built the city of Harappa and is centered around a river in modern-day Pakistan.
2.r: Indus River Valley Civilisation [or Indus Valley Civilisation or Indus Civilisation, accept Harappan Civilisation before mentioned and prompt thereafter]

2.q: This country engaged in the "Great Marriage Debate" after its leader encouraged men to marry highly educated women. This country's government has a matchmaking office called the Social Development Unit which is intended to reverse the declining birth rates caused by its earlier "Stop at Two" family planning policy. This country was founded after being expelled by Tunku Abdul Rahman from a Federation that also included (*) Sabah and Sarawak. High pay for government officials to prevent corruption and the use of caning were among the measures used to take this country "from the Third World to the First World in a single generation" by its leader Lee Kuan Yew. For 10 points, name this wealthy city-state on the tip of Malaysia.

At one of these events, Meredith Hunter was killed by a member of the Hells Angels serving as a security guard.
